text:
In late August 1854, cholera swept through Soho, a crowded district of London, and within about ten days it had killed several hundred people living within a few streets of one another. Cholera is a disease that causes violent vomiting and diarrhea, and it can drain a healthy adult of fluid so quickly that death may follow within a day or two. At the time nobody knew what caused it. The prevailing view among physicians and officials held that diseases like cholera spread through "miasma", a poisonous vapor said to rise from rotting waste and foul ground. Germs had not yet been shown to cause illness, and the idea that a tiny living organism could make a person sick was still a minority opinion.

John Snow, a physician who lived and worked in Soho, did not accept the miasma theory. He had already given anesthesia to Queen Victoria during childbirth, so he was no obscure figure, but his ideas about cholera had won little support. During an earlier epidemic in 1848 and 1849 he had reasoned that the disease must be swallowed rather than inhaled, because its symptoms struck the gut first and not the lungs. He thought it passed from the waste of the sick into the water or food of the healthy. He had published this argument in 1849, and most of his colleagues had politely ignored it.

When the 1854 outbreak began around Broad Street, Snow saw a chance to test his idea on a small, well-defined population. He set out to discover where the dead had lived and what they had in common. He obtained records of deaths from the local registrar and then went door to door, asking families how they had lived in the days before the illness struck. The pattern he found was striking. Nearly all the deaths were clustered close to a public water pump on Broad Street, where residents drew water by hand for drinking and cooking.

Snow then looked for exceptions, because exceptions can break a theory or strengthen it. A workhouse near the pump, home to hundreds of poor residents, had suffered remarkably few deaths. When Snow investigated, he learned that the workhouse had its own well and did not depend on the Broad Street pump. A brewery on the same street reported no cases among its workers, who were given free beer and, it seems, rarely drank from the pump. These absences were as informative as the clusters.

He also found cases that seemed to contradict his map but in fact supported it. A woman who lived far from Broad Street had died of cholera, and her death puzzled him until he learned that she had liked the taste of the water from that particular pump so much that she had a supply carried to her home each day. Her niece, who drank the same water, died as well. Other people who lived farther away had children who attended school near the pump and drank from it. In case after case, the link ran through the water, not through the air of the neighborhood.

Snow also examined the water itself under a microscope and with chemical tests. The results were not conclusive, since the instruments of the day could not reveal the true culprit, but the water did look different from that of other sources. What persuaded him more was the weight of the evidence he had gathered about people's movements and habits.

On the evening of September 7, he presented his findings to the local board of guardians, the body responsible for the parish. He asked them to remove the handle of the Broad Street pump so that no one could draw water from it. The guardians were not convinced by his theory, but they agreed to act, and the handle was taken off the next day. By then the epidemic was already declining, as many residents had fled the area and many of the most vulnerable had already died, so the removal of the handle cannot be said to have ended the outbreak by itself.

Snow's work did not end there. He drew a map marking each death with a small bar at the address where it occurred, so that the heavy concentration around the pump could be seen at a glance. Later investigation traced the source of the contamination to a cesspool, a pit for household sewage, that lay very near the pump's well. A baby in the house at 40 Broad Street had died of what appears to have been cholera shortly before the outbreak, and her family's waste had probably leaked into the water supply through a decaying brick lining.

Official inquiries at the time largely rejected his conclusion, and many authorities remained loyal to the miasma theory for years. Yet his method, combining careful counting, mapping, and the search for revealing exceptions, laid foundations for modern epidemiology, the study of how disease spreads through populations. Later work, including the discovery of the cholera bacterium, confirmed that he had been right, and Snow is now remembered as one of the founders of public health.
